Duration::min¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Duration Duration::min(bool skipna = true) const;

Smallest Elapsed Value¶

min() reduces every lane of the receiver to one scalar Duration. It is a global reduction: a matrix does not retain axes, and there is no dimension parameter. Comparison occurs directly in signed nanoseconds, preserving full integer precision.

skipna=true ignores NaT lanes. With skipna=false, any NaT makes the result NaT, which is useful when completeness is part of the validity of the answer. Empty input and all-NaT input have no finite candidate and return a scalar NaT; they do not throw.

The receiver is not mutated. The result always has rank zero and one logical element, including the no-candidate cases.

Examples¶

Example 1. Reduction crosses every axis and skips NaT by default.

auto values = pluss::duration::nanos(
    {5, pluss::Duration::kNaT, -2, 9}, {2,2});
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(values.min());

Output¶

Duration(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1)
-1 days 23:59:59.999999998

Example 2. Require every lane to be present.

std::cout << pluss::duration::print(values.min(false));

Output¶

Duration(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1)
NaT

Example 3. All-NaT and empty inputs converge on the same no-candidate result.

auto all_nat = pluss::duration::nanos(
    {pluss::Duration::kNaT, pluss::Duration::kNaT});
auto empty = pluss::duration::nanos(std::vector<std::int64_t>{});

std::cout << pluss::duration::print(all_nat.min()) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(empty.min());

Both results are scalar NaT, not empty arrays. This makes the reduction’s return shape independent of the number of input lanes.

See Also¶

  • max(): global maximum with the same NaT policy.

  • sort(): retain all values in ascending order.
